questions.cardText:
[Psychology] According to evolutionary psychology, why are females choosier than males in dating?
A. Due to the different costs of becoming a parent
B. Due to different opportunity costs in finding another mate
C. The difference is sociocultural and cannot be explained by evolution
Answer: A. Accordingly, the minimal parental investment or what is required to produce viable offspring is much higher for females than for males. This makes it optimal for females to be more selective, while males may benefit from “investing” more widely.
questions.de: Welche 1972 von Robert Trivers benannte Theorie erklärt die größere Wählerischkeit von Weibchen bei der Partnerwahl mit den für sie höheren Mindestkosten, lebensfähigen Nachwuchs hervorzubringen?
questions.en: Which theory, coined by Robert Trivers in 1972, explains females' greater choosiness in mating by the higher minimal cost to them of producing viable offspring?

timeline.labelEn: Robert Trivers coins parental investment theory: the sex that invests more in offspring is choosier about mates
timeline.labelDe: Robert Trivers prägt die Theorie des elterlichen Investments: Das Geschlecht, das mehr in Nachwuchs investiert, wählt Partner sorgfältiger

questions.notes: The card's answer (different costs of becoming a parent) is Trivers' parental investment theory per Wikipedia; question reworked to name the theory.

questions.cardText:
[Physiology and Anatomy] What is the largest human organ?
A. Heart B. Skin C. Liver
Answer: B.
questions.de: Was ist das größte Organ des menschlichen Körpers?
questions.en: What is the largest organ of the human body?

timeline.labelEn: Andreas Vesalius publishes De humani corporis fabrica, the founding work of modern human anatomy
timeline.labelDe: Andreas Vesalius veröffentlicht „De humani corporis fabrica“, das Gründungswerk der modernen Anatomie des Menschen

questions.notes: Wikipedia: the skin is the largest organ in the human body, roughly 16% of body mass (the liver is the largest internal organ). Timeline: no date of its own; Vesalius's Fabrica (June 1543) as the founding description of human anatomy.
